seo.metaTitle: Convert PNG to LAB - Perceptual Lightness and Color Map
seo.metaDescription: Decompose an image into perceptual lightness plus the green-magenta and blue-yellow axes. Free and local, nothing is uploaded - the conversion runs in your browser.
seo.longDescription: LAB is the space built so that equal numeric steps look like equal perceptual steps. L is lightness on the familiar 0 to 100 scale, while a and b are two opponent axes - a runs from green to magenta and b from blue to yellow - each centered on zero, which is neutral gray. The values here are normalized into 0 to 1 with the axes centered at mid gray, because a PNG can only store three bytes per pixel. It runs in your browser on PNG, JPG, WebP and BMP files, uploads nothing, and keeps alpha intact.
howTo: Drop the image into the source area, or pick a file from your device.
Pick Component: L for lightness, A for the green-magenta axis or B for the blue-yellow axis.
Switch Display to Space as RGB to see all three as red, green and blue.
Download the result from the Download button.

faq.q: Why are a and b shown as brightness instead of signed numbers?
faq.a: A PNG channel cannot be negative. The green-magenta and blue-yellow axes are therefore centered at mid gray: 0.5 is neutral, darker means green or blue, lighter means magenta or yellow. That is a display choice, not a different measurement.

faq.q: How is LAB different from the HSL split?
faq.a: HSL numbers were built for convenience; LAB was built so that a difference in the numbers matches a difference you can see. Two colors at the same L in LAB really do look equally bright, where HSL lightness does not promise that.

faq.q: Do I need this for printing?
faq.a: No. LAB is the working space for color management, not an output format. For ink coverage use the CMYK page, and for a print-ready file convert in an editor that can embed an output profile.

faq.q: What happens to very dark pixels?
faq.a: The conversion follows the standard sRGB curve first, so shadows lift much more than a plain average would. That is deliberate - it matches how the eye reads brightness - but it means the L map of a dark photo carries more detail than the raw channels.
